newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe's Mugabe pledges more privatisations. [CORRECTED 09:18 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe's Mugabe pledges more privatisations. [CORRECTED 09:18 GMT]

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe pledged on Wednesday (corrects from Thursday) night more privatisation of loss-making state firms following the successful public offer last month of the national dairy, Dairibord Zimbabwe Ltd (DZL).

"The process of privatisation by government continues. That is really coming...," Mugabe told industrialists during a question and answer session at the annual Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) congress in the northern resort town of Victoria Falls.

"We would want to see what has happened in Dairibord happen also with regard to the other parastatals we are working on and the same process will take place there," he said, giving no timetable and no further details.
Industry sources however say the national carrier Air Zimbabwe and the Cotton Company of Zimbabwe were due to be privatised later this year.
Mugabe's government has been under pressure from Western donors bankrolling its economic reforms to privatise loss-making state firms.
The public offer of 75 percent of DZL was the first major move on a privatisation programme which has been on the drawing board for the past seven years.

The offer, which included some private allocation of shares to the state National Investment Trust set up to promote the government's plans to economically empower the majority black population, was 10 times oversubscribed.
Mugabe said he expected more individual black investors to benefit from further privatisations.

Asked if the government planned to dispose of its remaining 25 percent stake in DZL, Mugabe said it would continue to hold onto it until it was satisfied about the company's successful operations as a private enterprise.

Earlier, opening the CZI congress, Mugabe said his government would try, in the second phase of its economic reforms yet to be implemented, to complete the reorientation of fiscal policy and public enterprise reform by strengthening expenditure management and prudently managing the financing of its spending deficit.
Economic analysts and local industrialists say high government borrowing from the domestic market to finance a widening budget deficit was crowding out the productive sector.
The government's budget deficit is expected to rise to 11 percent of Gross Domestic Product in the financial year ended June 30, missing a target of 8.5 percent.
